The maturation of high-throughput biology over the past two decades has transformed multi-omics from an opportunistic by-product of profiling a sample with several platforms into an explicit analytical discipline. Where early studies tended to concatenate single-omics outputs at the level of figures or supplementary tables, contemporary cohort and single-cell studies increasingly require that molecular layers be modelled jointly so that shared regulatory programmes, modality-specific responses and missing-data patterns can be disentangled in a principled way [R2, R5, R40]. This shift has been driven by a steady expansion in the number of layers that can be measured routinely — bulk and single-cell transcriptomics, epigenomics, proteomics, metabolomics, metagenomics, metatranscriptomics and spatial modalities — and by the recognition that most biologically interesting phenotypes arise from interactions across these layers rather than from any one of them in isolation [R55, R56, R59]. Yet the empirical evidence that integration outperforms well-designed single-omics analysis is itself context-dependent: a recent colorectal cancer benchmark reported that a canonical similarity-network fusion method still produced the best subtype classification among eight integrative clustering tools, yet its margin over the best single-omics baseline was highly dataset-dependent, illustrating that added layers do not automatically deliver added insight [R17]. Integration, in other words, is not an end in itself; it is a methodological choice whose value must be defended against well-controlled unimodal alternatives.

The practical consequences of treating integration as a discipline rather than a postscript are now visible across the software landscape. Generic spreadsheets and monolithic pipelines struggle on three fronts simultaneously: sample coverage is rarely balanced across modalities, data formats are heterogeneous even within a single project, and the analytical workflows required to move from raw features to interpretable models are long enough that their conclusions are sensitive to undocumented parameter choices [R1, R10]. The result is a well-documented reproducibility crisis in which re-running a published multi-omics analysis rarely yields identical biological conclusions, even when the input data are unchanged. This concern is sharpened in microbiome and host-microbiome settings, where metagenomic, metatranscriptomic, metabolomic and host-response layers each have their own conventions, ontologies and batch-effect structures that must be reconciled before any joint modelling is meaningful [R1, R6, R8, R39]. It is sharpened again in clinical cohorts, where the cost of re-analysis mistakes is highest and where standards such as FAIR data objects and reproducible workflow runtimes are now expected rather than aspirational [R27].

A second consequence is that software itself has become a first-class research output. Methods papers now routinely compete on the basis of architectural choices — whether a tool exposes a unified multi-assay data structure [R45], whether it scales to single-cell modalities [R4, R13, R26], whether it can be replayed through a workflow manager [R27, R43], or whether it offers a graphical interface that lets clinician-scientists participate without writing code [R9, R16, R23, R41]. At the same time, the proliferation of specialised tools has produced a fragmentation problem: a typical integrative analysis can plausibly call on a matrix-factorization method, a network-based meta-analyser, a pathway-level integrator and a deep-learning embedder, yet there is little consensus on how these pieces should be composed, and the conceptual framework that ties them together is often left implicit [R40]. Even when a conceptual scheme exists, its assumptions about independence between modalities, sparsity of the signal and tolerance for missing data are not always made visible to the user [R19, R31, R35], which complicates both interpretation and reuse.

This review therefore treats software as the primary object of comparison. We survey general-purpose integration frameworks and methods, microbiome-centred tools, web servers and point-and-click platforms, and the data structures and workflow systems that underpin reproducibility, before focusing in detail on EasyMultiProfiler (EMP), a recently published R workflow that uses the SummarizedExperiment and MultiAssayExperiment classes to deliver a five-module pipeline (extraction, preparation, support, analysis, visualization) for microbiome and host-microbiome studies [R1]. Throughout, we apply a consistent comparative lens that asks what each tool assumes about the data, what integration strategy it implements, what evidence supports its performance claims, and how those claims are qualified when examined critically. The goal is not to rank tools, but to make the design space legible so that users and developers can choose — or build — software whose assumptions match the biological question at hand.

The literature on multi-omics integration has converged, almost by convention, into a three-stage taxonomy that distinguishes the moment at which information from multiple assays is combined. In the early-integration paradigm, also termed concatenation-based integration, features from all omics layers are merged into a single design matrix and analysed with one model that treats features as exchangeable predictors under the assumption of joint observation over the same samples. The mixOmics R package provides a canonical realisation through sparse PLS and its multi-block extension DIABLO, in which partial least-squares components are fitted on concatenated feature matrices and forced to be correlated across blocks through a design matrix [R3, R44]. Closely related are model-based concatenation approaches that embed multi-omics data into a single likelihood, such as early multi-kernel classifiers or deep joint encoders, but the conceptual commitment is identical: features are made to see one another as if they originated from a single assay. A persistent weakness of this class is that it imposes a single metric and a single noise model on layers whose scales, sparsity and dependence structures differ profoundly; pre-processing choices therefore dominate downstream conclusions, and the literature is conspicuously thin on systematic comparisons of those choices.

Intermediate integration postpones the moment of fusion. Joint dimensionality reduction and matrix or tensor factorisations infer a small set of latent variables that approximate all omics matrices simultaneously: MOFA is the canonical example, using a Bayesian factor-analysis framework whose factors are shared across modalities and are interpretable in terms of both common and assay-specific variance [R2]; its single-cell extension MOFA+ applies the same logic through variational inference and flexible sparsity priors [R4]. Related matrix-factorisation-based clustering methods, such as multi-layer NMF, deep semi-supervised NMF (SSD-MO) and transfer-learning extensions of MOFA, explicitly factorise modalities into shared and residual components [R12, R19, R50]. Network-based intermediate integration offers a geometric alternative: Similarity Network Fusion constructs a sample-similarity graph per modality and fuses them through message-passing, producing a single affinity matrix that can subsequently be clustered [R5]. The advantage over concatenation is that each modality retains its own geometry; the disadvantage is that the resulting latent space or fused graph no longer carries the original features, complicating biomarker attribution and forcing users into post-hoc loadings analyses.

Late, or decision-level, integration keeps each omics layer analytically separate until the very end, combining only outputs — predictions, scores or rankings — across modalities. The simplest realisation is an ensemble of single-omics classifiers whose votes are aggregated, but the literature now extends this idea to multi-modal Bayesian uncertainty estimation, as in TMODINET, where each omics-specific predictor contributes through Dempster-Shafer fusion rather than naive averaging [R24]. Late integration is the natural choice when modalities are simply not co-measured, when one modality is very small, or when each omics platform already has its own gold-standard pipeline whose parameters should not be perturbed. The cost is that cross-omics interactions inside a single sample cannot in principle be recovered without at least one intermediate step somewhere in the workflow.

Cutting across these three stages are two orthogonal axes that are often elided in tool papers. The first is supervision: MOFA is unsupervised [R2], DIABLO is supervised by design [R44], and a family of recent variational and supervised factor models, including SigMAE, explicitly couples dimensionality reduction with prediction in a single optimisation [R35]. The second axis is data-driven versus knowledge-driven integration. Data-driven methods seek latent structure without recourse to prior biology, and most factor and matrix-factorisation work, including MOFA and SNF, falls into this category [R2, R5]. Knowledge-driven approaches compress features into pathways, networks or curated ontologies before integration: PathIntegrate, for example, scores samples against pathway databases prior to multi-view modelling, and the OmicsNet module of the Analyst suite performs biological-network integration as a third step after single-omics and data-driven integration [R29, R23].

The taxonomy, while pedagogically convenient, is not as crisp as the labels suggest. DIABLO is variously described as "early" and "intermediate" in different papers depending on whether the design matrix or the block structure is emphasised, and supervised variants of MOFA collapse the unsupervised/supervised axis onto what should be a separate methodological decision [R44, R2]. Terminology is also unstable across tool papers: "joint dimensionality reduction", "matrix factorisation", "multi-view learning" and "integration" are used almost interchangeably, which is one reason why head-to-head benchmarks frequently disagree on what counts as a baseline. More importantly, the practical choice among strategies is dictated less by algorithmic novelty than by data structure. Matched samples with low missingness favour intermediate factor or network fusion [R2, R5]; high sample-to-feature ratios favour concatenation or supervised PLS [R3, R44]; block-missing data almost force late integration or pathway-level aggregation [R29, R24]; and very small cohorts may require transfer-learning enhancements before any of the above will work reliably [R50]. These contingencies go a long way towards explaining why no single dominant workflow has emerged from the methodological literature, and they caution against treating any one integration strategy as universally preferable.

General-purpose integrative frameworks and methods for multi-omics data span at least four overlapping algorithmic lineages, each with a distinct conceptual take on what "integration" should mean. They differ sharply in input expectations, scalability, and what counts as a published tool versus a one-off pipeline, and a candid reading of the literature shows that the gap between methodological novelty and reproducible, well-engineered software remains large.

The factor-analysis lineage is dominated by Multi-Omics Factor Analysis and its descendants. The original MOFA infers a set of latent factors that capture both shared and modality-specific variation across heterogeneous omics layers and supports downstream tasks such as sample subgrouping and imputation [R2]; MOFA+ generalises this to multi-modal single-cell data using variational inference and flexible sparsity priors, allowing joint modelling across sample groups and modalities [R4]. A more recent addition is MOTL, a transfer-learning extension that augments MOFA-style joint matrix factorisation by borrowing latent factor structure from a large heterogeneous "learning" dataset to improve factorisation of limited-sample target data, with validation on simulated data and glioblastoma samples [R50]. The transfer-learning formulation is conceptually appealing in settings with few samples, but its gain over plain MOFA is intrinsically tied to the relevance of the source dataset to the target — a dependence that is rarely probed in head-to-head terms, and that cautions against uncritical adoption across biological domains.

The PLS-based integrative lineage is essentially the mixOmics family. mixOmics provides a coherent R package for feature selection, dimension reduction and integration of multiple omics assays through sparse PLS and related variants [R3]. Its supervised extension DIABLO identifies correlated subsets of discriminating molecular features across assays and phenotypic groups, offering modular and cross-over study designs and competitive predictive performance relative to supervised approaches while improving biological relevance over unsupervised integrative baselines [R44]. MixOmics has had demonstrable reach beyond cancer, including in plant abiotic-stress workflows for vertical and horizontal integration of phenomics, metabolomics, proteomics and transcriptomics [R33], which makes it one of the few general-purpose frameworks with broad-domain traction. Its main limitation is conceptual: linear projection in supervised mode can be sensitive to confounded designs, and feature selection on sparse PLS components remains a perennial source of reproducibility discussion.

A third lineage concentrates on similarity-network fusion. The canonical SNF method constructs per-data-type patient similarity networks and fuses them into one integrative network, achieving substantial gains over single-data-type analyses on five cancer datasets [R5]. MUUMI unifies statistical meta-analysis with network-based integration by combining SNF with interactome inference to identify robust molecular signatures [R10]. DeepMoIC embeds SNF into a deep Graph Convolutional Network trained on autoencoder-extracted representations for cancer subtyping [R28], while MINGLE uses sparse network estimation to merge multi-omics information into an integrated network for glioma heterogeneity [R49]. The intellectual coherence of this lineage is appealing, but fusion methods are highly sensitive to the choice of similarity metric and to the propagation of hub nodes, and most published implementations do not expose the network's sensitivity to these choices in a transparent way.

Deep matrix and tensor factorisations form a fourth stream. SSD-MO combines semi-supervised learning with multi-layer deep non-negative matrix factorisation and reports 7-24 % F-score improvements over baselines on six TCGA cancer datasets [R12]; MLMF integrates multi-layer linear/nonlinear factorisation with consensus fusion and a class-indicator matrix to handle partially missing omics, benchmarked across twelve multi-omics cancer datasets [R19]. GeDGC learns shared latent representations together with cluster factors through Gaussian mixture priors, while imposing a graph-embedding constraint to preserve cell-cell structure in single-cell multi-omics data [R13]. MCluster-VAEs further couples attention-based VAEs with a clustering objective, end-to-end, and is benchmarked against twelve other multi-omics clustering methods on TCGA datasets [R38]. These models are often impressive on TCGA but interpretability is uneven, and like most deep factorisations they inherit TCGA-tuned hyperparameters.

Graph-neural-network approaches are gaining ground. BioNeuralNet is presented as a modular Python framework for end-to-end network-based multi-omics analysis using GNNs to learn low-dimensional embeddings for downstream tasks [R11, R18]. MOGOLA combines GCN/GAT intra-omics feature extraction with a gating and cross-omics attention fusion mechanism, reporting gains over eleven state-of-the-art methods on BRCA, KIPAN, ROSMAP and LGG benchmarks [R52]; MO-GCAN trains per-omics GCNs whose embeddings are concatenated and re-fused through a graph-attention sample network across eight cancer types [R47]. TMODINET couples self-attention with adaptive graph dynamic learning and Dirichlet/Dempster-Shafer uncertainty estimation for trustworthy cancer diagnosis [R24]. Even the most carefully engineered GNN pipelines remain challenging to configure in low-data regimes, and current architectural diversity outpaces agreed-upon protocols.

Attention-based deep architectures and probabilistic models round out the catalogue. MOADLN applies self-attention to construct patient correlations before classification, outperforming several baselines on KIRP, KIRC, and related TCGA multi-omics tasks [R34]; CAEncoder combines a Vision Transformer with CycleGAN in an end-to-end contrastive framework for cancer detection [R48]; MOKAN adapts Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks with learnable edge-weight activations and subspace decomposition to capture inter-omics heterogeneity [R14]. On the probabilistic side, POPLS-DA provides a workflow that jointly analyses transcriptomics, proteomics and drug-screening data through a probabilistic PLS-DA formulation [R32]; NetMIM uses a spike-and-slab Bayesian prior with gene-pathway information and FBM-style data augmentation to handle block-missingness in multi-omics cohorts [R31]; PathIntegrate transforms multi-omics data to single-sample pathway scores before applying single- or multi-view predictive models [R30]; SigMAE fuses dimensionality reduction with predictive modelling in a supervised variational Bayesian factor setting [R35]; STATegra offers a conceptual multi-stage framework combining component analysis, non-parametric combination and exploratory analysis on TCGA glioblastoma and melanoma data [R40].

The critical reading that emerges is sobering. First, input expectations are highly heterogeneous: some tools expect matched-sample matrices, others expect graphs, others expect labelled and unlabelled samples simultaneously, which means their "head-to-head" comparison is often a category error. Second, despite the proliferation of methods, the recurring lack of independent, cross-domain head-to-head evaluation means that apparent superiority on TCGA is not yet transferable evidence; a recent benchmarking effort on unsupervised integrative clustering in TCGA colorectal cancer, for example, found SNF gave the best subtype classification accuracy [R17], which raises uncomfortable questions about whether the wave of newer deep matrix factorisations and GNN frameworks actually improve on simpler baselines once evaluation is done outside the authors' own protocol. Third, methodological novelty continues to outpace reproducible software engineering: containerised releases, version pinning, and FAIR packaging remain the exception rather than the rule for these general-purpose frameworks [R27]. Finally, the TCGA-centred benchmark culture is itself questionable — cancer cohorts are large, matched across modalities, and well understood, which is the opposite of the regimes (small cohorts, block-missingness, single-cell resolution, non-model organisms) where many users actually work. Until the community invests in independent, domain-stratified benchmarking and treats software quality as a first-class scientific deliverable, comparative performance claims in this literature should be read with conspicuous caution.

Microbiome-centred multi-omics tools occupy a distinct niche from general-purpose integration frameworks, reflecting the unusual statistical and biological constraints of community-scale data. Taxonomic and functional profiles derived from 16S rRNA amplicons, shotgun metagenomics, metatranscriptomics, metaproteomics and community metabolomics are compositional, sparse, and inherently hierarchical through phylogeny — properties that violate the Gaussian and independence assumptions common to methods developed for bulk transcriptomics or single-cell modalities. The earliest generation of microbiome software did not attempt integration at all but solved the prerequisite problems of reproducible import, manipulation and visualization of census tables. phyloseq established an object-oriented R/Bioconductor framework for importing, subsetting and graphically exploring operational taxonomic unit, sample-data and phylogenetic-tree objects, and it remains the de facto low-level data layer on which many downstream analyses are built [R6]. QIIME 2 generalised this logic into a plugin-based, artefact-centric platform with semantically typed data objects and provenance tracking, providing reproducibility and interoperability for amplicon and shotgun workflows at scale [R8]. Web servers such as MicrobiomeAnalyst layer a curated knowledge base and a panel of common statistical routines over these core data structures, lowering the barrier for users who lack programming expertise and supporting 16S, metagenomic and metatranscriptomic profiles as essentially single-omics inputs [R9]. Each of these systems excels within its own data type but, with the partial exception of MicrobiomeAnalyst's metatranscriptomic module, none was designed to ingest host-side molecular profiles alongside microbial ones, and none models cross-kingdom latent structure.

True meta-omic integration within microbial communities has therefore required purpose-built software. metaQuantome addresses the protein-level layer, providing statistical and quantitative routines for mass-spectrometry-based metaproteomics together with extensions that align metatranscriptomic measurements against the same functional hierarchy [R42]. This functional-axis harmonisation is a genuine advance over single-kingdom pipelines, but its integration logic remains one of mapping and comparison rather than joint latent-factor modelling, and the tool does not natively accommodate host-derived molecules. gNOMO extends the principle to non-model host-microbiome systems, integrating metagenomic, metatranscriptomic and metaproteomic layers from organisms that lack curated reference databases and bundling the workflow as a Snakemake pipeline for reproducibility [R43]. Its existence is itself a useful indictment of the field: the general multi-omics ecosystem, anchored by packages such as mixOmics and SNF-based methods, was built around well-annotated human and cancer data and required a bespoke solution to be repurposed for environmental and symbiont communities [R3, R5].

Longitudinal sampling is the norm in microbiome research and adds a further constraint that general multi-omics tools handle only patchily. PALM aligns multi-omic time series with irregular sampling, uses dynamic Bayesian networks to model interactions among taxa, genes, metabolites and host expression, and validates the resulting network against inflammatory bowel disease data, including targeted experimental confirmation of a subset of predicted interactions [R39]. timeOmics provides a more generic Bioconductor framework for longitudinal multi-omics integration through preprocessing, modelling and clustering, demonstrated on integrative Human Microbiome Project diabetes data that include gut taxa alongside host molecular layers [R36]. Together these tools recognise that microbiome composition drifts on timescales that are short relative to host physiology, and they explicitly propagate this temporal structure into their statistical models — a feature almost entirely absent from latent-factor tools developed for static cohorts.

EasyMultiProfiler (EMP) enters this landscape as a workflow rather than a single algorithm, using SummarizedExperiment and MultiAssayExperiment as its storage substrate and organising functionality into extraction, preparation, support, analysis and visualisation modules [R1]. Its principal contribution is to package the disparate upstream processing tools and the downstream cross-omics analyses behind a single, reproducible interface, lowering the cost of going from raw reads to a host-microbiome model in one environment. The motivation for such a workflow is reinforced by clinical reviews emphasising that treat-to-target management of diseases such as IBD requires the joint interpretation of metagenomic, metatranscriptomic, viromic, metabolomic and host proteomic signals over time, with explicit attention to analytical validity and external calibration [R55].

The limitations should be stated candidly. EMP's analytical modules inherit the assumptions of their underlying algorithms, several of which — ordination, differential abundance, network construction — do not directly address compositionality or phylogenetic autocorrelation, and the workflow does not replace specialised longitudinal or causal-inference frameworks such as PALM or timeOmics. MicrobiomeAnalyst, gNOMO and metaQuantome are largely confined to microbial layers, with host integration added externally rather than modelled jointly. Across the microbiome-centred ecosystem, the dominant gap is precisely what motivates cross-kingdom integration: phylogenetic and compositional structure is treated as a data-cleaning concern, while host and microbial signals are coupled through concatenation or post-hoc correlation rather than through a statistical model that respects their distinct geometries. The available evidence does not show that any single current tool closes this gap; the realistic conclusion is that microbiome multi-omics analysis still requires deliberate stitching of microbial-aware ingestion, longitudinal modelling and cross-kingdom integration, of which EMP is the most coherent but not yet a complete solution.

Web servers and graphical interfaces occupy a critical niche in the multi-omics ecosystem by lowering the programming barrier for biologists and clinicians who would otherwise be excluded from integrative analysis. The Analyst suite, with its linked components for metabolomics (MetaboAnalyst [R7]), general omics (ExpressAnalyst, OmicsAnalyst) and knowledge-driven network integration (OmicsNet), exemplifies the design philosophy of providing a structured analytical path from raw data through single-omics analyses to joint dimensionality reduction and biological network interpretation [R23]. By formalising the workflow in a Nature Protocols contribution [R23], the developers frame accessibility as contingent not only on a friendly interface but also on transparent documentation of each analytical step, embedding reproducibility as a prerequisite for clinical translation. MetaboAnalyst 6.0 in particular extends metabolomics single-omics analysis with MS2 fragment-level annotation, complex multi-factor designs and metabolite–phenotype causal inference, while remaining operable entirely through a browser [R7]; this breadth makes it a frequent first stop in microbiome multi-omics pipelines where host or microbial metabolites carry substantial interpretive weight.

A parallel ecosystem has been built around the microbiome community. MicrobiomeAnalyst [R9] consolidated what had previously required stitching together QIIME 2 [R8] for upstream processing, phyloseq [R6] for taxonomic object handling and bespoke R scripts for differential abundance, into four browser-accessible modules covering marker-gene and shotgun metagenomic/metatranscriptomic analysis. Its reliance on community-standard knowledge bases and statistical routines allowed very rapid uptake by groups lacking dedicated bioinformaticians. Yet, as with MetaboAnalyst, the depth of integration is best characterised as a curated slice of well-established methods rather than a complete reimplementation of the underlying statistical machinery; the user is implicitly committed to the developers' choice of normalisation, transformation and multiple-testing correction. The natural complement to single-omics web interfaces is a code-based but relatively accessible multi-omics workflow such as EasyMultiProfiler [R1], whose SummarizedExperiment and MultiAssayExperiment containers expose the same data structures underpinning several of these web GUIs.

Recently, general-purpose web and Streamlit-based platforms have proliferated. Profiler [R16] presents itself as an open-source, modular Python/Streamlit suite spanning proteomics, transcriptomics, lipidomics and even EEG data, integrating quality control, statistics, machine and deep learning, biomarker discovery, pathway enrichment and survival modelling. Its offer of the same environment both as a hosted web service and as a local container represents a notable step beyond the typical server-only deployment. Similarly, MuSA [R41] exposes the MultiAssayExperiment data structure through a Shiny interface specifically tailored to radiogenomic breast-cancer datasets, allowing researchers without R proficiency to perform pre-processing, correlation, clustering and feature selection on heterogeneous radiomic and molecular layers. The single-cell analyst [R20] pushes the multimodal envelope further by supporting six single-cell omics modalities — scRNA-seq, scATAC-seq, immune profiling, copy-number variation, cytometry and flow cytometry — together with spatial transcriptomics, with more than twenty interactive tools running in the browser.

Network-oriented multi-omics has its own dedicated platforms. MONGKIE [R46] pioneered integrated network visualisation and analysis for glioblastoma multi-omics by combining a Java-based visualisation unit with clustering and over-representation algorithms, enabling interactive mining that static command-line workflows struggle to match. NOODAI [R51] formalises a network-based pipeline in which representative differentially abundant or expressed traits from each omics layer seed a joint interaction network analysed by the MONET decomposition tool, revealing central elements that bridge omics layers. Disease-specific portals extend this logic to clinical translation, exemplified by CPMOAD [R22], which integrates uniformly processed RNA-seq, DNA methylation and curated interaction data for preeclampsia with interactive differential-expression, methylation and pathway-enrichment modules. Such platforms demonstrate that accessible interfaces can serve as stable supplementary-material repositories, allowing the figures and tables generated in the underlying study to be regenerated and inspected interactively long after publication.

The accessibility-versus-depth trade-off, however, is real and largely unresolved. Web implementations typically reimplement a thin statistical slice of published algorithms, often without preserving the original authors' exact default parameters or convergence diagnostics. Version drift is acute: a tool running today may not implement the same parameters as the version on which a published study was based, and the absence of immutable containerised builds means that figures rarely survive bit-perfectly into the reproducibility record. Most platforms also impose practical data-size limits — Profiler, MetaboAnalyst and MicrobiomeAnalyst all warn that inputs beyond tens of thousands of features or large single-cell matrices must be summarised or batched upstream — and uncertainty quantification is either absent or reduced to crude permutation heuristics rather than the Bayesian or bootstrap procedures available in dedicated R or Python frameworks such as MOFA/MOFA+ [R4] or mixOmics. Containerised local deployment, which would mitigate many of these concerns, remains the exception: Profiler is one of the few to offer both web and desktop endpoints [R16], while CPMOAD [R22], NOODAI [R51] and MONGKIE [R46] rely on a hosted service model that cannot be replicated offline. The evidence therefore does not show that any single web platform provides the methodological depth of a dedicated command-line framework; what it does demonstrate is that such platforms are indispensable for reproducible supplementary material, for rapid clinical-translation pipelines where turnaround time matters more than algorithmic nuance, and as on-ramps that bring experimentalists into the multi-omics conversation before they graduate to programmatic workflows such as EasyMultiProfiler [R1] or MOFA+ [R4].

The pace of algorithmic innovation in multi-omics integration has decisively outstripped the maturation of the substrate on which integration software rests. New factor-analysis, matrix-factorization, graph-neural-network, and Bayesian models appear every month, yet the field's binding constraint is reproducibility rather than novelty: any analysis is only as trustworthy as the chain that produced, stored, versioned, and documented the data, code, and dependencies on which it depends [R27]. This observation reframes the technical comparisons in the sections that follow. Container classes that preserve assay/sample relationships, workflow managers that pin software environments, and FAIR-aligned packaging collectively determine whether a "result" is a number or an artefact. The heterogeneity of multi-omics studies — unequal sample coverage across assays, modality-specific preprocessing, and longitudinal or spatially correlated designs — magnifies this problem and explains why container-based frameworks such as SummarizedExperiment and MultiAssayExperiment [R45] have become the de facto coordination layer across the Bioconductor ecosystem, and why EasyMultiProfiler (EMP) [R1] deliberately re-uses them rather than introducing new structures.

The MultiAssayExperiment class, originally introduced to coordinate representation, storage, and operation on multiple genomics assays and instantiated at scale across The Cancer Genome Atlas as ready-to-analyze objects [R45], establishes a small but powerful contract: each experiment object carries matched sample and assay maps, with subsetting operations that preserve identities across modalities. Microbiome science reached a comparable inflection point earlier through phyloseq [R6], and EMP extends the principle by treating 16S, metagenomic, metatranscriptomic, metaproteomic, and host-transcriptomic layers as first-class assays within a MultiAssayExperiment skeleton [R1]. The decision is consequential because it inherits, at no implementation cost, a decade of subsetting, batch-correction, and differential-testing conventions already validated in oncology and metabolomics pipelines such as those built around mixOmics [R3, R33]. The analogous choice to package microbiome processing as reproducible, shareable QIIME 2 artifacts [R8] suggests an underappreciated convergence: whether the unit of exchange is an R/S4 object or a .qza file, the field is moving toward provenance-tracked containers that decouple data from any single toolchain. MultiAssayExperiment is not without caveats — its subsetting and colData consistency can be brittle when assays arrive from heterogeneous pipelines, and the class does not, by itself, enforce semantic alignment between modalities, leaving that responsibility with the analyst [R45].

Around these containers, workflow systems provide the operational envelope. Nextflow-based multi-omics pipelines packaged as FAIR Digital Objects and deposited in WorkflowHub demonstrate that reproducibility is achievable through explicit metadata, containerized execution, and machine-actionable manifests rather than through any specific integration algorithm [R27]. The implication is uncomfortable for work that equates methodological novelty with quality: a rigorously containerized DIABLO or similarity network fusion analysis [R44, R5] is more reproducible than a sophisticated deep-learning model whose training environment cannot be reconstructed. This separation of substrate from method is the reason EMP's modular five-stage architecture — extraction, preparation, support, analysis, and visualization — is implemented as a chained pipeline rather than as a single monolithic function [R1]: it allows users to swap individual modules, audit intermediate outputs, and re-enter the workflow at any well-defined point. The Snakemake-based gNOMO pipeline for host–microbiome meta-omics [R43] and the FAIR-packaged childhood externalizing behaviour workflow [R27] illustrate the same principle from different ecosystems, and their existence argues that the field's most consequential near-term advances are likely to be infrastructural rather than mathematical.

Longitudinal designs expose further weaknesses in generic infrastructure. MultiAssayExperiment does not natively encode time, so dedicated frameworks such as timeOmics [R36] and netOmics [R37] wrap the Bioconductor container with explicit temporal alignment, smoothing, and clustering steps, while PALM extends dynamic Bayesian network inference to longitudinal metagenomic, metatranscriptomic, metabolomic, and host-expression layers in inflammatory bowel disease cohorts [R39]. EMP, focused on microbiome research, does not currently advertise time-aware wrappers comparable to timeOmics; users with longitudinal host–microbe cohorts must therefore compose EMP with an external temporal module, which is a real limitation for studies in which time is the central biological axis [R1, R36].

These observations crystallize a critical point: reproducibility infrastructure is necessary but not sufficient. A MultiAssayExperiment object cannot detect a mislabelled sample, a Nextflow manifest cannot validate a phenotype codebook, and a container cannot adjudicate a contested biological interpretation [R45, R27]. The cumulative evidence nevertheless indicates that mature ecosystems (Bioconductor, QIIME 2, Snakemake/Nextflow) produce more reusable artefacts than heterogeneous ad-hoc pipelines, and that EMP's deliberate anchoring on Bioconductor classes [R1] places it on the more durable side of that divide — at the real cost of a steeper learning curve for users without prior Bioconductor exposure and at the more subtle cost of inheriting all of Bioconductor's release-cycle constraints.

Empirical benchmarking in multi-omics integration has matured unevenly across disease areas and data modalities, and the evidence base that users actually rely on is narrower than the volume of published tools would suggest. In solid tumours, the most rigorous integrative-clustering benchmarks to date remain those anchored to TCGA. A systematic evaluation of eight unsupervised multi-omics integrative clustering methods on simulated and real TCGA colorectal cancer data — integrating methylation, gene expression and protein expression — found that Similarity Network Fusion produced the most accurate subtype classification, although no single method dominated across all metrics, and performance was highly sensitive to the correlation structure imposed on the simulated data [R17]. Importantly, the authors emphasised that synthetic benchmarks with engineered cross-omics correlations inevitably favour methods that exploit those specific structures, and that external validation against independent cohorts remains the decisive test. In a complementary clinical setting, application of Multi-Omics Factor Analysis to a 335-patient breast cancer cohort with transcriptomic, proteomic and metabolomic profiling identified three long-term prognostic clusters whose survival divergence extended beyond five years and was replicated in METABRIC and TCGA, lending biological and clinical credibility to a clustering solution that purely in silico accuracy metrics cannot establish [R25].

The single-cell literature has produced the largest and most transparent benchmarks, and these deserve to be read with both appreciation and caution. A comprehensive evaluation of 14 protein-abundance and chromatin-accessibility prediction algorithms and 18 single-cell integration algorithms across 47 datasets singled out totalVI and scArches for protein prediction, LS_Lab for chromatin-accessibility prediction, and Seurat, MOJITOO and scAI/UINMF-family methods for integration as the most consistent performers [R26]. While such breadth is unusual and welcome, the benchmark is still dominated by datasets in which cell-type identities are well characterised, where batch effects are tractable, and where the ground truth is largely defined by the very annotation practices that integration algorithms are designed to recover. None of these conditions is typical of a clinical tumour microenvironment or an understudied tissue, and performance rankings therefore should not be assumed to transfer. Reviews of deep-learning approaches in tumour genomics reinforce this caveat, noting that convolutional, recurrent, graph and attention-based architectures are typically evaluated on the same handful of TCGA and METABRIC splits, with hyperparameters tuned by the developers themselves and rarely audited independently [R56].

A second, structural weakness of the current benchmarking literature is that sample sizes, missingness patterns and class imbalance almost never match the conditions under which multi-omics tools will eventually be deployed. Many cancer benchmark studies pool a few hundred TCGA samples across highly imbalanced subtypes, while real-world cohorts frequently have tens of cases per class, block-missing omics layers, and skewed covariate distributions. Benchmarks that simulate block-missingness or use matched full-case subsets can demonstrate algorithmic robustness in principle but cannot substitute for evaluation in prospectively accrued cohorts. Large prospective clinical platforms such as SCRUM-Japan MONSTAR3 — designed to enrol 400 patients with newly diagnosed or relapsed/refractory hematologic malignancies and to integrate whole-exome, transcriptome, spatial transcriptomic, plasma proteomic, metabolomic, microbiome and minimal-residual-disease data — therefore function as an essential, complementary evidence layer [R15]. Their value is not to crown a clustering or classification algorithm but to expose whether a tool's signal survives the noise of clinical sampling, pre-analytical variability and the regulatory constraints of a routine diagnostic pipeline.

What the benchmarks do not show is equally consequential. They rarely, if ever, demonstrate that a tool's output predicts a clinically actionable endpoint — response to a specific therapy, durable remission, transplant eligibility — beyond a survival hazard ratio. Subtype classification accuracy, F-score improvements of 7–24 percent over baselines, or batch-corrected silhouette coefficients are not clinical endpoints, and treating them as such is a recurrent methodological error. Downstream biological validation — replication in an independent cohort, mechanistic follow-up in models, prospective demonstration that an algorithmic subgroup receives differential benefit from a targeted intervention — should be treated as the gold standard against which any benchmark metric is interpreted. Integrated clinical platforms that couple standardised wet-lab protocols with multi-layer molecular profiling and curated outcomes are the most credible setting in which this validation can occur, and they should be viewed as the arbiters of benchmark utility rather than as yet another dataset to be mined [R15].

For microbiome-specific workflows, where benchmark datasets are particularly scarce and reference materials are still maturing, this caution applies with extra force. Until dedicated, prospectively collected host-microbiome multi-omics benchmark cohorts become available, evaluation criteria must privilege transparent preprocessing, principled handling of compositionality and missingness, and demonstrable biological interpretability over headline accuracy on synthetic or repurposed case-control collections.

EasyMultiProfiler (EMP) is presented as a unified R workflow that addresses the long-standing fragmentation of microbiome multi-omics analysis by wrapping heterogeneous tools inside a coherent framework built on the SummarizedExperiment and MultiAssayExperiment Bioconductor classes [R1]. Its architecture decomposes a typical pipeline into five interconnected modules — data extraction, preparation, support, analysis and visualisation — invoked through a natural-language-style interface so that the user does not have to manage incompatibilities between upstream taxonomic profilers and downstream statistical engines. In the landscape reviewed in earlier sections, this places EMP closer to the multi-omics framework MultiAssayExperiment [R45] and the Analyst software suite [R23] than to a single integration algorithm such as MOFA+ [R4] or SNF [R5]: EMP is principally a workflow and integration layer, not an integration method in itself.

The choice of SummarizedExperiment and MultiAssayExperiment as foundational containers is, on the criteria of data-structure soundness and reproducibility, a defensible one [R1, R45]. These classes formalise sample alignment across assays, enforce row- and column-wise metadata, and inherit Bioconductor's unit-testing and release conventions. By anchoring itself to them, EMP inherits the same provenance tracking, batch-aware accessors and ready-to-analyse objects that already power TCGA-scale cancer multi-omics work [R45]. The same cannot be said of pipelines implemented purely in ad hoc Python or Snakemake scripts without typed container classes, where reproducibility depends entirely on workflow-manager pinning and external checksum capture [R27]. EMP's reliance on Bioconductor's typed objects therefore offers a meaningful reproducibility advantage over many microbiome-centric tools that pre-date this convention, and brings microbiome multi-omics into structural alignment with general-purpose Bioconductor infrastructures.

For algorithmic breadth, EMP is best characterised as a curated wrapper. The five-module design accommodates taxonomic and functional profiling, differential abundance, network analysis, time-series modelling and visualisation, drawing on — rather than re-implementing — components such as mixOmics-based PLS/DIABLO integration [R3, R44], timeOmics-style longitudinal modelling [R36], netOmics-style network interpretation [R37] and metaQuantome-style metaproteomic and metatranscriptomic quantitative analysis [R42]. Compared with phyloseq [R6], which excels at object-oriented single-omics census analysis but does not natively integrate host-omics layers, EMP explicitly targets the host-microbiome interface. Compared with QIIME 2 [R8], a self-contained plugin ecosystem oriented around sequencing features, EMP is lighter on raw data processing and heavier on cross-omics synthesis. Compared with MicrobiomeAnalyst [R9], EMP trades point-and-click accessibility for programmability and reproducibility; compared with PALM [R39], a dynamic Bayesian network pipeline for longitudinal IBD multi-omics, EMP offers broader algorithmic coverage but less depth in causal temporal modelling.

Domain specificity is where EMP makes its strongest claim. The workflow is microbiome-centric rather than universal, designed to handle metagenomics, metatranscriptomics, metaproteomics and metabolomics alongside host expression [R1]. This focus distinguishes it from the cross-domain MultiAssayExperiment framework [R45], from single-cell multi-modal tools such as MOFA+ [R4] and from generic platforms such as Profiler [R16] or BioNeuralNet [R18], and aligns it more directly with gNOMO [R43] for non-model host-microbiome meta-omics and with PALM [R39] for longitudinal human microbiome cohorts. The longitudinal support emphasised in EMP's design also overlaps with what timeOmics [R36] and netOmics [R37] offer; however, those packages are method-focused rather than container-focused and must be embedded in a wrapper such as EMP, or in a mixOmics-driven workflow chapter [R33], to become truly end-to-end.

A candid critical assessment is, however, necessary. The evidence presented in support of EMP is largely descriptive: the demonstration cases illustrate that the workflow can be run, not that it outperforms alternatives on quantitative benchmarks such as subtype recovery, integration error or computational cost [R1]. Recent benchmark studies for general multi-omics integration — such as comparisons of integrative clustering methods on TCGA colorectal cancer data [R17] and large-scale benchmarking of single-cell multi-omics prediction and integration algorithms [R26] — show that the field increasingly judges methodological novelty by such quantitative comparisons. EMP's novelty lies substantially in the assembly and in its natural-language-style interface rather than in new statistical machinery, and the paper does not demonstrate that the assembled workflow is faster, more accurate or more statistically powerful than running mixOmics [R3], timeOmics [R36] or netOmics [R37] individually. EMP is therefore best read as a convenience and reproducibility layer for microbiome researchers rather than as a methodological advance.

Two further limitations follow from this design philosophy. Because EMP is microbiome-centric, transferring it to non-microbiome problems — for example to plant abiotic-stress multi-omics workflows built around mixOmics [R33] or to TCGA-style cancer multi-omics [R45] — is not its intended use case, and users in those settings should prefer more general Bioconductor infrastructure. Moreover, the validity of any EMP result depends on the validity of the underlying components; algorithmic improvements elsewhere, such as newer graph-based or contrastive deep-learning frameworks [R11, R48], will not automatically propagate into EMP unless re-invoked through its interface. In summary, EMP is best positioned as a principled, microbiome-aware orchestrator of existing Bioconductor and R multi-omics machinery — a useful complement to, rather than a replacement for, the specialised frameworks discussed in earlier sections.

The most uncomfortable starting point for any critical assessment of multi-omics software is the field's own admission that no gold standard exists. Borisov and colleagues state plainly that "there is still no consensus on a gold standard protocol for the integration of various multi-omics profiles into a uniformly shaped system bioinformatics platform" [R21], an acknowledgement that is striking for its bluntness and that recurs implicitly across nearly every comparative study in this space. The proliferation of methods — matrix factorisation variants, similarity-network fusion, deep latent-variable models, attention-based fusion, Kolmogorov–Arnold networks, graph neural networks — has not converged on a canonical pipeline; instead, every new method is benchmarked against an ever-shifting set of baselines, each claiming superiority on its preferred cohorts. The result is a literature in which "state-of-the-art" is essentially a moving target defined by the latest publication rather than by durable evidence.

A second, tightly linked controversy is the near-total dominance of TCGA-derived benchmarks. Recent comparative work in colorectal cancer relies exclusively on TCGA methylation, expression and protein data [R17]; semi-supervised deep matrix factorisation methods are evaluated on six TCGA cancer cohorts [R12]; MOGOLA is benchmarked on BRCA, KIPAN, ROSMAP and LGG [R52]; and even MOFA+ applications to long-term prognostic subtyping in breast cancer are validated back onto METABRIC and TCGA [R25]. This self-referential validation loop inflates the apparent portability of methods that, when transferred to non-TCGA cohorts, often degrade. The single-cell benchmark of Hu and colleagues, which evaluated 18 integration algorithms across 47 datasets and found that "overall totalVI and scArches outperformed" the field but with substantial dataset-dependent variability [R26], is the closest the field has come to a non-TCGA-centric evaluation. Performance instability across disease contexts is therefore not a peripheral concern but a structural feature of how methods are selected and rewarded. Methods that perform well on bulk TCGA solid tumours are routinely applied without evidence of efficacy to haematologic malignancies [R15], extracellular-vesicle biomarkers [R54], reproductive disorders [R53] or non-model host-microbiome systems [R43], despite obvious biological and technical differences.

Reproducibility is the third fault line, and one on which recent reviews have been unusually candid. A review of AI for exosomal biomarker discovery in cardiovascular disease explicitly highlights reproducibility limitations arising from non-standardised isolation, pre-analytic variability and dataset heterogeneity [R54]; reviews of spatial multi-omics catalogue technical noise, batch effects and calibration drift as unresolved challenges [R59]; and surveys of AI in viral and stem-cell multi-omics repeatedly invoke the same shortcomings without offering remediating tooling [R57, R58]. The conceptual review of cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic syndrome outlines a multidimensional biomarker framework without specifying integration software, which is itself an indictment of the immaturity of current tooling relative to the conceptual ambitions [R60]. When the same review-level evidence is invoked across disease domains to flag the same deficiencies, it becomes clear that reproducibility is not a disease-specific problem but a field-wide failure of standardisation that existing software does not solve.

A fourth controversy is the methodological opacity of black-box deep models. The critical review of deep learning in tumour genomics catalogues CNN, RNN, GNN, autoencoder and transformer architectures applied to mutation detection, expression profiling, methylation prediction and integrative multi-omics, but the very diversity of architectures masks a common deficit: post-hoc interpretability is treated as optional rather than as a release criterion [R56]. Newer frameworks such as Kolmogorov–Arnold network-based models [R14], graph neural network pipelines [R11], graph-embedded deep generative clustering [R13] and semi-supervised deep matrix factorisation [R12] report quantitative gains on TCGA cohorts but offer little insight into the biological provenance of their latent dimensions. Even when attention or gating mechanisms are introduced ostensibly for interpretability [R47, R52], validation is typically limited to ablation studies rather than to perturbation or experimental confirmation. The data, in short, do not show that these models capture biologically meaningful mechanism — only that they fit held-out benchmarks.

A fifth tension concerns the gap between integrative clustering and clinical actionability. Sharma and colleagues show that even when MOFA+ identifies multi-omics clusters with distinct long-term prognoses in breast cancer, these do not align cleanly with clinically deployed intrinsic subtypes [R25], raising the question of what additional decision-making value they provide. Reviews of multi-omics in inflammatory bowel disease emphasise that analytical validity, external validation, calibration and action-linked thresholds remain aspirational rather than operational [R55]. Method benchmarks typically optimise internal metrics — silhouette scores, F-scores, AUC — that are detached from the regulatory and clinical questions a treating physician actually needs to answer. Until software developers engage with clinical decision thresholds, prospective validation and cost-effectiveness, integrative clustering will remain a research exercise rather than a clinical instrument.

Finally, the unresolved tension between generalist and domain-specific ecosystems is itself a controversy. mixOmics [R3], MOFA+ [R4], MultiAssayExperiment [R45] and SNF [R5] aim for breadth across organisms and modalities; EasyMultiProfiler and MicrobiomeAnalyst concentrate on microbiome-specific workflows [R1, R9]; single-cell platforms such as the single-cell analyst [R20], Profiler [R16] and Seurat-based pipelines serve yet another community. Reviews of reproductive, viral and stem-cell multi-omics each survey a different combination of these tools [R53, R57, R58] without convergence. The critical view — and one that the evidence here supports — is that generalist tools sacrifice biological fidelity for portability while domain-specific tools sacrifice methodological generality for fit. Neither side has won, and the field has not yet articulated criteria by which the trade-off should be resolved for a given scientific question. Until it does, the publication of yet another benchmark study claiming state-of-the-art status on TCGA will continue to add to a literature that is large, technically sophisticated and clinically still largely unmoored.

For users, the most consequential decision is to resist algorithmic novelty in favour of fit-for-purpose matching between integration strategy, data structure and scientific question. When the goal is unsupervised discovery of shared variation across quantitative assays, joint matrix factorization remains a defensible default; transfer-learning variants such as MOTL address the recurrent small-sample problem in clinical multi-omics cohorts, while supervised Bayesian factor models such as SigMAE are preferable when labels exist [R35, R50]. For predictive or classification tasks with deep architectures, the single-cell benchmark by Hu and colleagues demonstrated that no single algorithm dominates across data regimes and that totalVI, scArches, LS_Lab, Seurat and MOJITOO each excel in different settings, so algorithm choice should be guided by the modality mix and sample size rather than by reported peak accuracy on a single dataset [R26]. For pathway-level biological interpretation, multi-view PLS approaches such as DIABLO and the more recent PathIntegrate convert molecular features to pathway scores before modelling, which is closer to the mechanistic language clinicians expect and is more readily transferred across cohorts [R30, R44]. Microbiome-oriented projects should think of EMP as one component of an ecosystem rather than a single entry point: its MultiAssayExperiment backbone aligns it with the wider Bioconductor infrastructure [R1, R45], but vertical integration with metagenomic-specific packages such as phyloseq and QIIME 2 and with metabolomics-specific web tools such as MetaboAnalyst remains necessary for complete pipelines [R6, R7, R8].

A second priority concerns the data structures on which any tool sits and the reproducibility infrastructure that surrounds them. Methods built directly on stable, well-curated container classes inherit the long-term maintenance, validation and community tooling that come with Bioconductor and SummarizedExperiment derivatives; the longevity of MultiAssayExperiment since its introduction is itself evidence of the value of this design choice [R45]. Workflow systems that package analysis steps as FAIR Digital Objects, such as the Nextflow multi-omics workflow distributed as a Research Object Crate via WorkflowHub, demonstrate how versioning, containerisation and provenance can be made first-class rather than aspirational [R27]. Users should therefore prefer tools with version-pinned releases, containerised execution and explicit metadata schemas, and should treat web servers as exploration and entry points only: platforms such as MetaboAnalyst, MicrobiomeAnalyst, the Analyst suite, Profiler and NOODAI are excellent for triage and teaching but cannot substitute for reproducible command-line analysis once projects move beyond pilot scale [R7, R9, R16, R23, R51].

Third, evaluation criteria must move beyond clustering accuracy. The reported 7–24% F-score gain of SSD-MO over baselines on six TCGA cancer datasets is informative, but the benchmark itself does not show comparable gains on non-cancer, longitudinal or microbiome data, and the colorectal-cancer comparison that found SNF superior should not be read as a verdict that similarity-network fusion is universally best, but rather as evidence that dataset characteristics and evaluation design drive the apparent ranking [R12, R17]. The field should converge on biologically validated outcomes — replicated signatures in independent cohorts, mechanistic concordance with curated pathways, or patient-level clinical endpoints — rather than continue to rely on synthetic or single-cohort benchmarks. Several limitations remain under-characterised in the existing literature: how transfer-learning gains in MOTL depend on the choice of source dataset is not quantified in the original study, how graph-neural-network approaches such as BioNeuralNet, MO-GCAN and MOGOLA inherit the well-known instability of cell–cell graphs under sparsity is rarely characterised, and how uncertainty estimates are reported remains inconsistent across deep frameworks, with most offering no principled quantification at all [R11, R24, R47, R50, R52].

For developers, three priorities emerge. First, publish as FAIR Digital Objects with explicit container and version metadata, following the model of the Nextflow multi-omics workflow rather than relying on README-style installation instructions [R27]. Second, participate in neutral, third-party benchmarks such as those conducted for single-cell integration, since self-reported comparisons on a single dataset are increasingly unconvincing [R26]. Third, report uncertainty explicitly, as TMODINET does through Dirichlet and Dempster–Shafer estimation, rather than presenting point predictions without any confidence statement, and document failure modes rather than only favourable configurations [R24].

In closing, the field's near-term progress will be driven less by yet another deep architecture than by reproducibility, interoperability and biological validation. Positioned as one workflow among several addressing the microbiome niche, EMP offers a coherent R-based entry into host-microbiome integration that gains leverage from its MultiAssayExperiment foundation, but it is neither a universal solution nor a redundant wrapper around existing Bioconductor tools; its long-term value will depend on how seriously the community takes containerisation, FAIR packaging and biologically anchored benchmarking in the versions that follow.
